#0 The investment case

The conclusion. Reply is a high-quality IT services compounder priced at the 5th percentile of its own ten-year P/E range. Three dated reports in 2027 can re-rate it, and its €550m buyback lifts FY2027-28 EPS 5-8% above a consensus that still assumes a flat share count. The probability-weighted return is c. +30% over 18 months, with the odds about two to one in favour.

The one idea: Reply sells outcomes, so it keeps the AI productivity gain

Reply is a federation of about 300 small, specialised IT consultancies that sells complex digital and AI implementation work to large European enterprises. Italy provides c. 63% of revenue. Reply prices 71% of its revenue as fixed-price contracts and delivers 86% of its work onshore.

Because Reply sells outcomes rather than hours, the productivity that generative AI gives its developers (up to 30% of man-days) lands first in Reply's margin rather than on the client's invoice. That structure explains why Reply's EBITDA margin (18.8% in 2025, c. 18% underlying) is five to nine points above the margins of Capgemini, Alten and Sopra Steria, while its organic growth (8.0% in Q2 2026) is three to eight points higher.

The same structure sets the main risk. Reply's contracts last 6-24 months, so if clients learn to demand the AI saving back at renewal, a few points of price on 71% of revenue fall almost straight to profit. Because Reply gives no guidance, the market learns which way this is going only two quarters at a time.

The change: three positive forces outweigh one structural headwind

  1. Enterprise AI demand has moved from pilots to production (Reply's CEO, 1 August 2026). Reply's organic growth re-accelerated from 6.6% in Q1 2026 to 8.0% in Q2 2026, while EPAM grew 3.5% and Globant shrank. The EU AI Act, the NIS2 cyber-security directive and the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) make a growing share of this spending non-discretionary.
  2. Reply is investing into AI demand at a pace no peer matches. It has launched 30-40 new AI start-ups since January 2026, built Model Factory and the Symbiosis operating model, gained NVIDIA Physical AI and OpenAI Advanced Partner status, and bought a margin-accretive US federal and defence business in July 2026. This investment costs margin now (Region 3 EBIT was minus €0.5m in Q2 2026) and pays back in 2027-28.
  3. Capital allocation has pivoted to a buyback. Management ruled out buybacks in March 2026, then launched a €550m programme (9.6% of capital) in April 2026. Reply had bought back c. €90m of shares by August 2026, yet consensus still models a flat share count.

The headwind is the sector-wide debate about AI deflating billable work. That debate took sector multiples to decade lows and Reply's shares from €168 (March 2025) to €90 (March 2026). The debate has not gone away; it has only stopped getting worse. Germany (mostly automotive and manufacturing clients, c. 18% of revenue) is only just turning, with organic growth of 5.5% in Q2 2026 after 0.8% in Q1.

How the change reaches the financials: almost all of the EPS gap to consensus is the share count

My revenue and margin forecasts sit close to consensus; my EPS forecasts sit above consensus because the buyback shrinks the share count.

  • Revenue grows c. 10% in FY2026 (c. 7.5% organic, plus the US acquisition in H2) and c. 8.5% in FY2027, close to consensus.
  • The group EBITDA margin holds at 18.1% in FY2026, because H2 is seasonally stronger than H1's 17.8%, and then climbs 20bp a year as the 2026 start-up cohort matures and Germany re-enters its 14-16% margin corridor.
  • The average share count falls from 37.3m to c. 34.5m by FY2028 as the buyback runs.

On these forecasts EPS is €7.81 / €8.86 / €9.83 for FY2026-28 (+15% / +13% / +11%), against consensus of €7.67 / €8.39 / €9.02. FY2027 and FY2028 consensus EPS therefore sits 5-8% too low, and nearly all of that gap is mechanical (the share count), not a view on demand.

The buyback is the unmodelled upgrade: €550m authorised (9.6% of capital), c. €90m done by August 2026, while consensus keeps the share count flat. Nearly all of the 5-8% gap to FY27-28 consensus EPS is the share count.

The upgrades should arrive at three reports. They are the FY2026 results on 16 March 2027 (H2 margin and treasury share count), the Q1 2027 statement in May 2027 (organic growth, including Germany) and the H1 2027 results in late July 2027. Reply gives no guidance to raise, so the market's "guidance" event is the consensus revision after each report. The narrative should shift from "AI victim with a premium multiple" to "fixed-price AI winner buying back a tenth of itself"; the sector digest notes of October-November 2026 already show that shift beginning.

The foundation: a long, clean record, with weaknesses in governance rather than in the business

Reply's record is long and clean. Over ten years revenue compounded at 14% a year, EPS at 16-18% and free cash flow at 19%; ROIC is c. 19%; the company has held net cash every year, presents no adjusted earnings and has made no restatements; employee turnover has fallen to 13.4%. Management (the Rizzante family; the CEO has led since 2006 and the CFO has been in the group since 1996) has beaten consensus EPS by high single digits in most recent quarters while meeting consensus revenue. The one recent miss was the Q4 2025 margin of 19.9% against 20.8% expected.

Why Reply outgrows its industry

  • Dense coverage of specialist niches
  • 80% of growth from existing clients
  • No client above 10% of sales
  • Boutique-level partner incentives optimised at a 20% margin

These features have let Reply outgrow and out-earn a weak industry structure for 25 years.

Weaknesses, real but of a different kind

  • Governance: the founder holds 69% of votes on 37% of capital; no nominations committee; CFO succession unclear
  • No quantitative guidance
  • An unannounced €50m acquisition
  • Partner-level P&L silos that former managers say hinder cross-selling
  • A small open criminal investigation (€2.9m provision)

The industry structure is unhelpful to most of the sector: it is fragmented, the hyperscale cloud providers are powerful, and partners cooperate in public while competing in private.

The setup: a cause for concern that is clearing, in a high-quality business on a bottom-quartile multiple

The best label for this setup is "cause for concern clearing, in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a bottom-quartile multiple, leading to reversion to normal". A strong secondary element is "delivering mechanical EPS upgrader", from the buyback.

Present

  • A well-identified cause for concern (AI deflation, plus German and French drag) drove the multiple to the 10th percentile and is now clearing on dated evidence: Q2 organic acceleration, the German rebound, consensus upgrades, and new sector price uptrends since 23 October 2026.
  • The Business Foundations report rates the business's quality highly.
  • The multiple is still at the 5th percentile of its own ten-year P/E range (13.9x against an 18.7x median).

Missing or weak

  • The cause for concern is structural, so no single report can cleanly clear it, and the multiple's reversion may stop short of the median.
  • The shares have already recovered 65% from the March 2026 trough, so part of the setup's reward has been taken.
  • Quality is high on financials but only medium on governance.
The multiple, not the earnings, is the case: 13.9x two-year-forward earnings, at the 5th percentile of its ten-year range, against a median of 18.7x and a Broadening guideline of 21.6x, while EPS has compounded at 16-18% a year.

The reward and the skew: about two to one in favour, resting on the multiple

The two-year-forward EPS on my forecasts rolls from €9.83 (FY2028) today to €10.84 (FY2029) in twelve months. On that EPS, the value of the shares depends mainly on the multiple:

  • At today's 13.4x (on my numbers) the shares are worth €145 (+12% with the dividend).
  • At my fair multiple of 17x they are worth €184 (+41%).
  • At the Phase guideline of 21.6x they are worth €234 (+80%).
  • If the case fails (organic growth of 4%, a 17% margin, EPS of c. €9.0 and a multiple of 11.5x) they are worth c. €104 (20)%.

Weighting the base case (50%, +41%), the better case (25%, +60%) and the worse case (25%, (20)%) gives c. +30% over 18 months. Three things support the floor: €402m of net cash (8% of market cap), a buyer in the market every month, and earnings that still grow in the worse case.

What has to be true: three tests, each with a dated check

  1. Growth: group organic growth stays at or above 7%, with Germany at or above 4%. The checks are the FY2026 results on 16 March 2027, the Q1 2027 statement in mid-May 2027 and the H1 2027 results in late July 2027; headcount growth at or above 5% is the leading indicator.
  2. Margin: the FY2026 EBITDA margin prints at or above 18.0% (H2 at or above 18.3%), Region 3 EBIT turns positive by H1 2027, and Region 2 EBITDA margin is back above 14% by H2 2027. The same three reports show all three.
  3. Buyback: the buyback runs at €12m a month or more, so treasury shares exceed 5% of capital by 16 March 2027 and the programme is more than half complete by end-2027. The monthly buyback notices and each report's treasury share line show the pace.

The five judgements that move the value most

The margin and AI-pricing judgements put the most EPS at risk; the multiple moves the value most of all.

  1. Organic growth. Each point of organic growth on c. €2.7bn of revenue is €27m of revenue; at a 30-35% incremental margin it is c. €9m of EBITDA, €6m of net income and €0.17 of EPS (c. 2%). If FY2027 organic growth falls from my 7% to Bernstein's 4% discard level, EPS is c. €0.55 (6%) lower and the multiple would revert toward 11-12x, a price of c. €100.
  2. Group EBITDA margin. Each 50bp of margin on FY2027 revenue of €2.96bn is €15m of EBITDA, c. €10m of net income and €0.29 of EPS (3.3%). The gap between Bernstein's long-run 16% margin and my 18.3% is 230bp, worth €68m of EBITDA and €1.30 of EPS (15)%.
  3. Buyback execution. The full €550m programme, completed by 2029, cuts the share count by c. 10%, and consensus includes none of it. Half execution would leave FY2028 EPS at c. €9.4 rather than €9.83 (4.5)% and FY2029 EPS at c. €10.2 (6)%.
  4. The multiple. Each turn of P/E on FY2029 EPS of €10.84 is worth €10.84 a share, 8.3% of today's price. A move from 13.4x to 17x adds €39 (+30%); 13.4x to 21.6x adds €89 (+68%); 13.4x to 11.5x removes €21 (16)%.
  5. AI price pass-through. If clients capture 3 points of price on the 71% fixed-price book across one renewal cycle, with no volume offset, revenue is c. 2% (€60m) lower on an unchanged cost base. Almost all of the lost revenue is lost EBITDA, c. €1.15 of EPS (13)%. The visible counter-evidence is 8% organic volume growth and clients reinvesting their savings (Bernstein, October 2026).

#1 Operating environment: a K-shaped market, with Reply on the rising arm

The environment supports c. 7% organic growth for Reply without heroics, but not a return to the 10%+ of 2021-23. Specialised, fixed-price, regulated-sector, onshore work is growing at high single digits while generic IT services grow 1-2%.

DriverEvidenceFor Reply
DemandEnterprise AI is moving from pilots to production (Reply's CEO; Deutsche Bank sector note, 15 October 2026: "back for good, at least for H2"). Gartner expects European IT services to grow 5.8% a year to 2030.Positive
IT budgetsMorgan Stanley's Q3 2026 CIO survey has total IT budgets +4.0% in 2026 and 2027 but IT services only +1.8%, because AI infrastructure crowds out discretionary services. European budgets grow 3.1%, with a near-zero recovery in services in 2027.Negative
Regulation and public spendingThe EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA and the EU sovereignty package turn compliance into non-discretionary multi-year projects. Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) lifts public IT budgets by c. 25%. Defence spending is rising.Positive
CompetitionAccenture grew 7% in Q4 FY26, beating its guidance; Capgemini's Continental Europe accelerated to +2.8%; Alten's Germany to +4.5%. Indian offshore providers are seeing compression.Mixed
Labour supplyHiring is "easier than a couple of years ago" (Reply's CEO); salary inflation is c. 3.5%.Positive
MacroEurozone GDP growth is 0.8-1.2%; the ECB is expected to tighten to 2.75%; French sovereign stress spilled into Italian spreads in October 2026. The FfF digest rates Italy's IT sector Underweight and reads the market regime as risk-off beneath the index.Negative
DisruptionAI code tools deflate hourly work; the hyperscale cloud providers are building forward-deployed engineering teams.Negative

Inference: weak sector numbers are a headwind for the narrative, not for Reply's volumes. Reply has outgrown the sector by 5-8 points in every period of the last three years. Reply faces two genuine headwinds. The first is AI price deflation at contract renewal, which moves slowly and is so far absent from Reply's contract data. The second is European macro (German industry, Italian spreads and interest rates), which is observable and currently stable to improving.

Counter-case. Morgan Stanley's 0.3% recovery in European services for 2027 is the market's base case. If AI budgets keep crowding out services and clients demand savings, Reply's 8% organic growth could become 4-5% within a year.

Market view versus mine. The sell-side (83% Buy ratings) agrees on Reply's relative position; the market multiple does not yet reflect it. I agree with the sell-side on direction, and I think the deflation risk is real but one to two years away for a fixed-price seller.

What changes my view: two consecutive quarters of group organic growth below 5%, or German organic growth below 1%.

Conclusion: tailwinds are moderate and selective and headwinds are structural but slow, so the net effect is favourable for a fixed-price specialist. The environment supports step 2 of the argument (the change) but caps its size at high-single-digit organic growth.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Enterprise AI moving from pilots to production plus regulation-driven, non-discretionary spend (AI Act, NIS2, DORA, PNRR, defence) support c. 7% organic growth for a fixed-price, onshore specialist that has outgrown the sector by 5-8 points, but the wider market is weak (IT services budgets +1.8%, near-zero European services recovery in 2027) and AI price deflation on renewal is a direct structural threat to the same demand; consensus sales growth at the 75th percentile fits a real but selective, partly offset net positive.

#2 Internally driven change: investing hard while peers cut, and buying back a tenth of the company

Two internal changes, Region 3's margin recovery and the buyback, are together worth more EPS than the whole of consensus EPS growth for FY2027-28. They are the main source of my EPS gap to consensus.

Evidence.

  • AI start-ups and products: 30-40 new start-ups since January 2026, 95% of them in AI (25 in Q4 2025 alone); Model Factory (sovereign model training); the Symbiosis operating model (October 2026); Neurons (agent orchestration); LEA (agentic logistics).
  • Partner status: NVIDIA Physical AI Specialization (one of the first globally); OpenAI Advanced Partner (through Cognita Reply); an AWS strategic collaboration and Agentic AI specialization; Microsoft Agent 365 launch partner; Mistral sovereign models (through Sail Reply).
  • Acquisitions and restructuring: a US federal and defence acquisition in July 2026 (c. €50m of annual revenue, margin-accretive according to the CFO); Solirius and Red Scientific in UK public sector and defence (Solirius has won over £100m of multi-year contracts); Movar and Cyberis. Wemanity (France) has been restructured and is nearing breakeven; the Breed Reply incubator has been liquidated. Management is now willing to consider a $200-300m US acquisition.
  • Capital: the €550m buyback, launched in April 2026 after management ruled out buybacks in March; the dividend raised 17% to €1.35.
  • Cost: subcontractors cut from 27% of sales (2023) to 17% (2026); headcount growth of 6.4%, below revenue growth; employee turnover of 13.4%.
  • Problems: Region 3 EBIT was negative in Q2 2026, and Region 1 and Region 3 margins fell year on year; the German margin is 12.9%; expert calls describe partner P&L silos; Reply discloses no quantified AI productivity; the buyback reversed earlier messaging.

Inference: Reply is investing hard into the technology cycle while peers cut, and it funds that investment without debt. The start-up drag is the price of the strategy, and it is visible, bounded and historically temporary.

  • Bounded: Region 3 is c. 20% of revenue, and the swing in its EBIT margin from c. 14% to c. 0% is c. €70m of annualised profit, the largest single recoverable item in the group.
  • Temporary: Reply's model has always launched units, given each two to three years, and replaced the management of those that miss their margin targets.
  • The buyback is the second internal change, and the one the market has priced least. At c. €15m a month the buyback retires c. 1% of the company each quarter.

So what: the internal forces are large relative to the market cap. Region 3 normalising is worth c. €1.0-1.3 of EPS over three years and the buyback c. €1.0 by FY2029. Together they exceed the entire consensus EPS growth for FY2027-28 (€7.67 to €9.02, or €1.35).

Region 3 normalising (c. €1.0-1.3 of EPS over three years) and the buyback (c. €1.0 by FY29) are together worth more than all the consensus EPS growth for FY27-28.

Counter-case. Bernstein argues that start-up creation "has not slackened since late 2025" and will keep margins range-bound. A large US acquisition could also dilute the buyback and consume the net cash.

Market view versus mine. Bernstein (Market-Perform) sees the start-ups as a margin problem; Deutsche Bank (Buy) models margins flat at 18.0-18.2%. Neither broker models the falling share count. I think the start-up drag is an investment phase that reverses from 2027, and that Reply's buyback is the cheapest upgrade in the sector.

What changes my view: a second half in which Region 3 EBIT stays negative, or a buyback pace below €8m a month.

Conclusion: the internal change is strong and well funded, with a measurable near-term cost and a 2027-28 payoff. It supports steps 2 and 3 of the argument and is the main source of my EPS gap to consensus.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. A funded, multi-part programme: 30-40 AI start-ups and partner certifications, a margin-accretive US federal acquisition, subcontractors cut from 27% to 17% of sales, and a EUR 550m buyback (about a tenth of the equity) started in April, worth together more than consensus EPS growth for FY27-28; it is held back because the start-up drag is in today's numbers (Region 3 EBIT negative, Germany at 12.9%) and the payoff is 2027-28 and unproven abroad, where Germany and France turned slowly.

#3 Value chain, business model, financial profile, management: the business model is the asset

Reply's federation model turns a structurally weak industry into 25 years of compounding. The financial profile is clearly above average; governance is a discount item, not a risk to cash flows.

Evidence: where Reply sits. Reply sits in the specialist-boutique tier of the IT services value chain (gross margin c. 35%, EBIT margin 14-16%), above the scaled integrators (EBIT margin 11-15%) and below the software vendors. Capex is under 2% of revenue.

Evidence: the industry. The industry is fragmented, and barriers to entry are low for boutiques, although onboarding with an enterprise client takes three to seven years. The hyperscale cloud providers hold 80% of the European cloud market and are moving into delivery, and clients are insourcing through global capability centres.

Evidence: Reply's position.

  • c. 300 boutiques in c. 20 clusters; 80% of growth comes from a larger share of wallet in existing accounts, encouraged by finder's fees for cross-selling.
  • The top ten clients are 29% of sales and none is above 10%. Microsoft is the second-largest client and the main partner (sales with Microsoft up 1.5x).
  • The average project is c. €0.8m, and contracts run 6-24 months.
  • Fixed-price work is 71% of revenue (82% in Italy, 35% in Region 3); offshore delivery is 14%, against 50-84% at the Indian providers.

Evidence: financial profile. In FY2025 revenue was €2.48bn, the EBITDA margin 18.8%, the EBIT margin 15.8% and net profit €251m. ROIC is c. 19% (Capgemini: 12.5%); net cash was €468m at year-end 2025; free cash flow conversion has been above 90% through the cycle; and the three-year revenue CAGR is 9.5% (Capgemini: 1.7%). Reply presents no adjusted earnings and expenses the amortisation of acquired intangibles. Its tax rate of c. 31.7% is a permanent Italian drag.

Evidence: management and governance.

  • The Rizzante family runs the company: the founder is Chairman and co-CEO, his daughter has been CEO since 2006 and his son is CTO. The CFO was promoted from within.
  • Pay is mostly cash and below the peer median. The long-term incentive is weighted 58% to EBIT growth and 26% to total shareholder return. Partner pay is optimised at a 20% margin and doubles at 22.5%.
  • Reply gives no guidance.
  • Through four votes per share, the family holds 69.4% of votes on 37.1% of capital (September 2026), so no activist can act. 60% of the board is non-independent, there is no nominations committee, and the CFO transition is ambiguous.
  • A €2.9m provision covers a 2017-19 computer-fraud investigation; there have been no restatements or control weaknesses.

Inference. Reply turns a structurally weak industry (price takers, dependent on the hyperscale cloud providers) into 25 years of compounding by keeping its units small, specialised, accountable and close to the client, and by pricing outcomes. That model is why the three "outliers" in the Business Foundations report coexist: growth through downturns, a high margin with low capital intensity, and a granular customer base. Governance is a discount item rather than a risk to cash flows, for three reasons: the family's economic stake is large, its incentives are profit-based, and its record of treating minority shareholders well (rising dividends, now a buyback) is good.

So what. The foundation supports a premium multiple to the sector: Reply has traded at 1.5-2x Capgemini's P/E for a decade. It also makes the "quality business at a cyclical trough" element of the setup credible.

Counter-case. The Leadership Foundations report notes that the CEO has never run anything outside the family firm, and expert calls describe silos and a weak brand outside Italy. Together these mean the model may not replicate abroad, and France and Germany are the evidence.

Market view versus mine. The market treats Reply as a high-quality name (Deutsche Bank: "best-in-class compounder") but prices it on sector fear. I agree on quality: I rate the operating model high quality and the governance medium quality.

What changes my view: a large US acquisition that stretches the model, or partners leaving after an integration.

Conclusion: Reply is an above-average business with a differentiated model and a strong financial profile, run by capable but entrenched owners. The foundation supports step 4 of the argument and underwrites the floor in the worse case.

Score: 71, set by the Rater. A differentiated federation model (small fixed-price boutiques, onshore, partner pay tied to margin, no client above 10%, 80% of growth from existing accounts) has compounded for 25 years with ROIC c. 19% (16.5% latest, 85th percentile), net cash and over 90% cash conversion, though EBITDA margin sits only at the 40th percentile on the latest year; the industry is fragmented with powerful hyperscalers and an open AI-disruption question that lowers predictability, and governance (69% of votes on 37% of capital, no nominations committee) is ordinary, so it sits below Tenaris's protected global share and above Volex.

#4 Guidance, expectations management, delivery record: Reply lets the sell-side set a low bar, then beats it on cost

Reply has an excellent delivery record against a sell-side that is habitually too low on margins. Because Reply gives no formal guidance, every upgrade must come through consensus after each report.

Evidence: guidance. Reply gives no quantitative guidance, only a qualitative 14-16% margin corridor for its regional units. The CFO refuses to disclose acquisition prices. Management declined to quantify AI productivity until October 2026, when analysts judged the CTO's fireside chat "much better constructed".

Evidence: delivery. Over the last four to five quarters Reply has met consensus on revenue and beaten it on EPS by high single digits (Q3 2025 EBITDA 7% above consensus; Q2 2026 organic growth of 8% against Bernstein's 6%). The one miss was the Q4 2025 margin of 19.9% against 20.8%. Redburn notes that sell-side margin forecasts have historically been too low. The dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum B.

Evidence: consensus. Over twelve months consensus EPS has risen 4.1% for FY2026 and 5.5% for FY2027, but FY2028 is 5.1% lower than a year ago. The FY2028 fall reflects the March 2026 cuts (Redburn cut its target from €175 to €125; Bernstein from €155 to €114), which brokers then partly reversed (Bernstein €121, Deutsche Bank €140; the FactSet mean target is now €161).

Inference. Reply does not manage expectations down; it lets the sell-side set them and then beats on cost. Two consequences follow. First, consensus margins are set conservatively: flat at 18.0-18.1% for three years, for a company whose partner incentives target 20%. Second, "guidance upgrades" do not exist as an event, so the upgrade cycle runs entirely through consensus after each report. The absence of guidance also explains the stock's violent swings in sentiment ((45)% in 2025-26 with no earnings cut): investors have no management number to anchor on.

So what. Reply's track record makes it probable that it beats FY2026-27 consensus modestly. The lack of guidance means the market will not believe the beat until Reply reports it, and that delay is the source of both the setup's return and its risk.

Counter-case. Redburn itself warns that the beat pattern may simply reflect low broker numbers, so a normalisation of estimates would remove the surprise.

Market view versus mine. Consensus assumes a flat margin and a flat share count; I assume both improve. On revenue I am 1% below consensus for FY2027-28, because I think the sell-side has extrapolated Q2's 8% organic growth further than the German and French evidence yet justifies.

What changes my view: a second margin miss within two years, or a move to issuing guidance that proves conservative (which would be positive).

Conclusion: an excellent delivery record and a habitually low sell-side margin forecast, offset by the absence of any formal guidance to raise. The record supports step 3 (how the change reaches estimates) and step 4 (the foundation).

Score: 66, set by the Rater. There is no quantitative guidance (neutral in itself); against consensus the record is revenue in line and high-single-digit EPS beats in most recent quarters, with one margin miss (Q4 2025, 19.9% against 20.8%) and a long, restatement-free decade of delivery, and FY26/FY27 consensus is up 4-6% over twelve months although FY28 was cut in March 2026 on sector fear. A good record of beating a habitually low consensus, but with no guidance actively kept conservative and one recent miss, it sits just below Linea Directa.

#5 Operating and financial leverage, pricing power, feedback loops: modest operating gearing, three extra levers

8% revenue growth should become 11-15% EPS growth a year through 2028: c. 8 points from revenue, 1-2 points from margin and 3-4 points from the falling share count.

Evidence.

  • Sensitivities (Deutsche Bank, Redburn): shown in the boxes below the chart.
  • Cost structure: personnel costs are 55.5% of revenue, and services and subcontractors 25%. Subcontractors are the flexible layer, cut from 27% to 17% of sales in three years.
  • Pricing: junior DevOps engineers bill at up to €150 an hour. Fixed-price contracts (71% of revenue) retain AI efficiency gains until renewal, but proof-of-concept work needs discounts. Italian salaries are rising 3.5%.
  • Financial: net cash earns treasury income (H1 2026 pre-tax profit +8.2% on EBIT +0.7%); there is no debt; the €550m buyback is under way.
  • Positive feedback loop: start-ups create niches, the niches are cross-sold into existing accounts (80% of growth), and those accounts fund more start-ups. Partner incentives double at a 22.5% margin.
  • Negative feedback loop: start-up payroll runs ahead of start-up revenue, which depresses margins until the units scale.

Inference: Reply's operating leverage is modest, but it has three levers most peers lack. As a people business Reply earns incremental margins of only 30-35%. Its three extra levers are the fixed-price capture of AI productivity, the flexible subcontractor layer, and a balance sheet that can retire a tenth of the equity without borrowing. The buyback is the purest form of financial leverage available to a net-cash company, and Reply is using it at a P/E of 13-14x, an earnings yield of 7% or more, well above the return on cash.

Counter-case. If AI deflation hits the fixed-price book at renewal, the same operating leverage works in reverse. Wage inflation above 3.5% would also compress the labour spread in an onshore model that has no offshore cost arbitrage.

Market view versus mine. Bernstein argues that competition will remove the AI gain; Redburn and Deutsche Bank argue that Reply retains it for the life of each contract. The evidence so far favours Redburn and Deutsche Bank: margins reached a ten-year high in 2025, and personnel costs grew more slowly than revenue in H1 2026.

What changes my view: the subcontractor ratio rising back above 25% of sales (the Business Foundations report's early-warning signal), or a fall in average revenue per employee (c. €153k).

Conclusion: operating leverage is moderate, financial leverage is strong and underused, and pricing power is contested but so far intact. This topic supports step 3 of the argument and supplies most of the double-digit EPS growth.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. As a people business the operating gearing is modest (personnel 55% of revenue, incremental margin 30-35%, 1% revenue moves EPS about 1%), but three gears add to it: fixed-price capture of AI productivity until renewal (contested pricing power), a flexible subcontractor layer, and a net-cash balance sheet retiring about 10% of the shares at a 7%+ earnings yield; EPS growth of 11-15% on 8% revenue is about 1.5 times, below the Universe's typical 2 times, so an ordinary-plus mix.

#6 Forecast financials: the same quality of growth, with a buyback added

My FY2026-28 EPS of €7.81 / €8.86 / €9.83 is 2% / 6% / 9% above consensus, almost entirely because of the share count; my revenue and margin sit at or near consensus.

Four test questions set these forecasts.

  • Delivery: the expected change (c. 7% organic growth, margins near 18%) is what Reply has demonstrably done through 2024-26. Nothing in my forecast needs a capability the business lacks, except the Region 3 recovery, where the record in Germany and France is of slow turnarounds.
  • Range of outcomes: the range is wide on the multiple and narrower on earnings. A plausible 18-month range for FY2027 EPS is €8.0-9.2 ((10)% / +4% around my €8.86).
  • Guidance: there is none to raise or cut. The risk of a consensus cut at any of the next four reports is c. 15-20%, driven by a German relapse or a margin miss.
  • Revisions: consensus revisions are more likely up than down (c. 55-60% up, 25% flat, 15-20% down), because consensus carries no buyback and flat margins.

These answers led me to hold revenue at or below consensus and to attribute almost all of my EPS gap to the share count.

The forecasts do not ask for faster growth than history. EPS grows at double digits through FY2029 on my numbers, but revenue does not, and the margin only returns to the underlying 2025 level (18.0%, excluding the provision reversal) plus 50bp. Over the past four years revenue compounded at 12% and EPS at 16%; the next four years are slower on both. The case is therefore not "higher growth than history"; it is "the same quality of growth at a multiple a third lower, with a buyback added".

Where I differ from the market is the share count alone. Consensus FY2028 EPS of €9.02 implies net income of €340m on c. 37.7m shares. My FY2028 net income of €339m is the same; the difference is my 34.5m shares. I cannot name evidence on demand that the sell-side lacks, so my revenue sits at consensus. I can name evidence the sell-side holds but does not model: the buyback programme, its H1 2026 pace and the treasury share count.

Conclusion: the forecasts are step 3 of the argument in numbers. They leave open one question: whether the market will pay for mechanically generated EPS.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. 10-15% gives B; placed low in the band because the growth is slower than the past four years (EPS CAGR 16%), the margin only returns to the underlying 2025 level plus about 50bp, and 3-4 points a year come from the buyback rather than the business (consensus EPS growth is only 7.9%, 32nd percentile), though revenue growth is organic and the base is clean.

#7 Scope for upgrades: mechanical first, with the share count the surest item

There is modest but well-founded scope for 3-8% upgrades to consensus EPS over 18 months, driven by the share count and the H2 margin rather than by demand surprises. These upgrades are the probable trigger for the multiple's reversion.

Not yet in consensus or the narrative.

  1. The buyback share count is worth +4-5% to FY2027 EPS and +8% to FY2028 at my assumed pace. The evidence is the €550m authorisation, €64m spent in H1 2026, c. 1m shares bought by August, and the CEO's statement that the balance sheet funds both the buyback and the acquisition pipeline.
  2. The FY2026 H2 margin: H2 is structurally stronger (19.3% in H2 2025) and the US acquisition is accretive. An 18.4% H2 margin gives FY2026 EPS of €7.81 against the €7.67 median, c. 2% higher.
  3. The German margin rising from 12.9% toward 14-15%: Region 2 revenue is c. €490m, so each point of margin is c. €5m of EBITDA and €0.10 of EPS. The evidence is the Q2 organic rebound to 5.5%; consensus's flat margins exclude it.
  4. Region 3 EBIT margin rising from c. 0% to 10% over 2027-28: worth c. €50m of EBIT and €1.0 of EPS, the largest item and the least certain. In favour is the model's history in Italy (21.7% margin) and France nearing breakeven; against stands the Fincon record in Germany.
  5. Treasury income is already in consensus (pre-tax profit +8% on EBIT +1%).

Already in consensus (momentum, covered in topic #8, not scope): the Q2 organic acceleration, the US acquisition's revenue (Deutsche Bank added 3% / 6% / 7% to revenue) and the FY2026 margin of 18.1%.

Probabilities over the next 18 months. Four reports fall in the period: FY2026 in March 2027, Q1 in May, H1 in July and Q3 in November. My probabilities for FY2027 consensus EPS are: up 3-6%, c. 55%; flat within 2%, 25%; cut by 3% or more, 20% (on a German relapse, a margin miss or a dilutive large US acquisition). Reply cannot raise guidance because it gives none, and its qualitative outlook is likely to stay "confident, in turbulent markets". The probability that the sell-side narrative moves from "premium multiple fully priced" (Bernstein) to "cheap compounder with a buyback" is better than even, provided the FY2026 results show an H2 margin at or above 18.3% and treasury shares above 5% of capital.

Counter-case. Bernstein's upgrade trigger is organic growth consistently above 10% or margin expansion outside Italy. Neither is in my forecast, so the most sceptical broker stays neutral even on my numbers.

What changes my view: a buyback pace below €8m a month (the buyback lever disappears), or Q1 2027 organic growth below 5%.

Conclusion: the scope for upgrades supports step 3 of the argument.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. There is no guidance to raise, so scope runs through consensus: the unmodelled buyback share count (+4-5% to FY27 EPS) and a stronger H2 margin give a likely raise of 3-6% (55% odds) against a 20% chance of a 3%+ cut, an expected move of roughly 2% on 8% revenue growth (about 0.25 times, near the 50th-55th percentile), with a narrative shift to 'cheap compounder with a buyback' likely if the March 2027 print delivers; the upgrade is mechanical and fairly sure but modest, so just below Helios Towers.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity: a simple case with one slow, hard-to-see risk

The near-term risks are trackable and cost 5-15% of EPS. The risk that matters most, AI price deflation on the fixed-price book, is slow and hard to observe from outside, and could cost 15-30% of EPS over two to three years.

Simplicity. Three drivers decide the case (organic growth, group margin and buyback pace), and Reply reports all three quarterly or monthly. Reply has no debt and no FX hedging to go wrong: it relies on natural hedges, and a 10% move in sterling is worth c. €0.09 of EPS. No customer is above 10% of sales, and no single contract matters. The bear case is equally simple: price deflation at renewal.

Fragilities and requirements.

  1. AI deflation on the 71% fixed-price book: slow, hard to observe from outside, and a "false friend" risk, because volume growth can mask erosion of unit prices. The Risks report puts c. 25% probability on the structural bear case, with downside to €61 (EPS of €5.50 at 11x).
  2. European macro: German automotive demand (automotive and manufacturing are c. 18% of group revenue), Italian spreads and interest rates; observable quarterly.
  3. Start-up and integration drag: observable in regional margins. Germany's margin fell from 19% to 13% after the Fincon acquisition, the precedent for slow turnarounds.
  4. A $200-300m US acquisition would consume the net cash, slow the buyback and add integration risk in a market where Reply's brand is weak.
  5. Governance and key-man risk: the founder, in his seventies, holds 69% of votes, and succession is opaque, although nothing is imminent.
  6. Disintermediation by the hyperscale cloud providers, and client insourcing: a multi-year risk, not an 18-month one.
  7. Legal: the €2.9m provision is immaterial.

Suddenness and precedents. The sector de-rates violently on sentiment: in 2003, 2009, 2020 and 2022, and in February-March 2026, when Reply fell 20% in weeks with no change to earnings. Reply's drawdowns were (50)% (2021-23) and (45)% (2025-26), and both recovered as earnings held. Because Reply reports semi-annually with quarterly statements and gives no guidance, the market sees a break in demand with a lag of one to two quarters.

Market view versus mine. The market still prices deflation as the most likely outcome: sector P/Es are 8-10x, and Reply trades at the 5th percentile of its own history. I price deflation as a one-in-four tail risk with a slow fuse, and both the fixed-price structure and the volume data argue against it.

What changes my view: average contract size trending below €1m, a rising subcontractor ratio, or group organic growth below 4% for two quarters (the Risks report's discard trigger).

Conclusion: a simple case of medium riskiness (B). This topic qualifies step 6 (the skew) and sets the triggers in step 7.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. The case rests on three trackable drivers (organic growth, group margin, buyback pace) with net cash and no customer above 10%, and the memo's FY27 EPS range is about (10)%/+4%, but one slow, hard-to-observe structural risk (AI price pass-through on the 71% fixed-price book, a 25% bear case at EUR 61), no guidance with semi-annual reporting, and a sector that de-rates violently on sentiment ((45)% in 2025-26 on no earnings cut) widen the equity outcome; better than Shell on balance sheet and cyclicality, short of Kerry's predictability.

#10 Lifecycle phase: turning up into early Broadening

The price has moved first, while upgrades and the narrative lag behind it. Reply sits near the start of the Broadening phase, which argues for a fair multiple below the Phase guideline.

The dashboard's rule places Reply in "Broadening". The evidence fits "turning up into early Broadening":

  • The trough (March 2026: €80, 10x) is eight months behind.
  • Consensus has turned up, but only by 2-6%.
  • The narrative has flipped from "AI victim" to "AI fixed-price winner" in the sector notes, but not yet in the mix of broker ratings (Bernstein and Intesa are neutral).
  • The price has recovered 65%, but the multiple is still at the 19th percentile of its five-year range and the 5th percentile of its ten-year range.
  • The 200-day average has risen for only four months.

A stock is "reinforcing" when upgrades, narrative and price feed each other and the multiple is in the top half of its range; Reply is not there yet. Reply would be "stalling" if the German recovery reversed or the March 2027 margin disappointed.

Market view versus mine. The dashboard and I agree on the phase. I would place Reply nearer the start of Broadening than the middle, and that placement argues for a fair multiple below the Phase guideline (topic #11).

Conclusion: the phase supports step 5 (the setup is live) and informs the fair multiple in step 6.

Score: 73, set by the Rater. The memo's 'turning up into early Broadening' is right and close to the computed Turning/Inflecting: the trough is eight months behind, organic growth has re-accelerated and Germany is turning, consensus is up only 2-6% with the buyback unmodelled, and the multiple is still at the bottom of its range, but the cause for concern is structural rather than cleanly cleared and the price has already recovered 65%, so early Turning with the thesis starting to broaden rather than confirmed Broadening.

#11 Fair multiple: 17x, the single largest judgement in the case

My fair multiple is 17x two-year-forward earnings over the next 6-18 months. The 21.6x guideline is the better-case ceiling, and 14-15x is the floor unless demand breaks.

The reference points. The guideline for the Broadening phase is 21.62x two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of Reply's own ten-year range (median 18.7x, 10th percentile 14.9x, 75th percentile 21.0x). Today's multiple is 13.9x on consensus and 13.4x on my FY2028 EPS.

Four reasons put my fair multiple below the guideline.

  1. The phase is early Broadening, and the guideline is written for a stock in peak delivery.
  2. The sector's AI deflation debate caps multiples across the group until a company discloses its fixed-price share and its deflation experience (the sector digest: "the first discloser becomes the reference"). The sector leaders trade at 8.6x (Capgemini), 9.3x (Sopra Steria) and 9.5x (Alten), so 21.6x would be a 2.3x relative premium, against a decade at 1.5-2x.
  3. Reply's margin is at a ten-year high and fell year on year in H1 2026, so the market will discount the risk that margins have peaked.
  4. The stock's own two-year median is 14.8x, so 17x already asks for a re-rating of a quarter.

The 21.6x guideline is reachable only in the better case, which requires organic growth back above 10% (Bernstein's upgrade trigger) and a disclosure that settles the deflation debate. I give that case a 25% probability.

Market view versus mine. The mean broker target of €161 on FY2027 EPS of €8.50 implies c. 19x one-year-forward earnings, so the sell-side's fair multiple is close to the ten-year median. Bernstein's €121 target implies c. 14x. My 17x sits between the two.

Conclusion: the fair multiple sets the reward in step 6 of the argument.

Score: 91, set by the Rater. Cheap on both gives A; placed near the floor because part of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year history was built at 14% revenue growth against about 8% now, the margin is near a ten-year high, and the AI-deflation debate caps sector multiples until it is settled, though a net-cash compounder still warrants more than 13.9x.

#12 Total shareholder return: +41% in the base case, c. +30% probability-weighted

The skew is favourable because earnings grow in every case and the multiple starts near its floor. Two-thirds of the base-case return comes from the multiple; with no re-rating at all, earnings and dividends still return c. 9-12% a year.

The arithmetic below is a Dupont split of my forecasts, anchored on two-year-forward EPS: FY2028 EPS of €9.83 today, FY2029 EPS of €10.84 in twelve to fifteen months, and c. €12.4 for FY2031 in three years (assuming 6% growth beyond FY2030).

Twelve to fifteen months (to early 2028)

  • Earnings growth: forward EPS rolls from €9.83 to €10.84, +10.3%.
  • Multiple: today 13.4x on my FY2028 EPS. At 17x (my fair multiple) +26.9%; at 21.6x (the guideline) +61.3%; unchanged, 0%.
  • Dividends: €1.55 paid in 2027, 1.2%.
  • Total at 17x: 1.103 x 1.269 - 1 = +40.0%, plus 1.2% = c. +41% (price €184). At 21.6x: 1.103 x 1.613 - 1 = +78%, plus 1.2% = c. +80% (price €234). At 13.4x: +10.3% + 1.2% = c. +12% (price €145).

Three years (to late 2029)

  • Earnings growth: €9.83 to c. €12.4, +26% (8% a year), of which c. 8 points come from the share count.
  • Multiple: at 17x +27%; at 21.6x +61%; at 13.4x 0%.
  • Dividends: €1.55 + €1.75 + €1.95 = €5.25, c. 4%.
  • Total at 17x: 1.26 x 1.269 - 1 = +60%, plus 4% = c. +64% (18% a year). At 21.6x: c. +107% (27% a year). At 13.4x: +26% + 4% = +30% (9% a year).

Probability-weighted over 18 months.

  • Base case (50%): FY2029 EPS €10.84 at 17x, +41%.
  • Better case (25%): organic growth of 9-10% and an 18.8% margin give FY2029 EPS of €11.0; at 19x the price is €209, +60%.
  • Worse case (25%): organic growth of 4%, a 17% margin and a halved buyback give FY2029 EPS of €9.0; at 11.5x the price is €104, (20)%.
  • Weighted: 0.5 x 41 + 0.25 x 60 + 0.25 x (20) = c. +30%.

What drives the return. Two-thirds of the base-case return is the multiple moving from the 10th percentile toward the median. The earnings leg is steady, and about a third of it is the buyback. Even with no re-rating the return is c. 9-12% a year, the floor that the net cash and the buyback make credible. The worse case loses 20% because it applies the 2026 trough multiple of 11.5x to a lower EPS that still grows. A fall to 10x on EPS of €8.5 (35)% would need a European recession.

Two-thirds of the base-case return is the multiple; even with no re-rating, earnings and dividends give c. 9-12% a year.

Market view versus mine. The sell-side mean target implies +23% in twelve months. My base case is higher because of the share count and a slightly higher multiple. My probability-weighted figure is close to the sell-side's because I carry a 25% downside case that the Buy ratings do not.

Conclusion: c. +41% in the base case and c. +30% probability-weighted over 18 months; c. 18% a year over three years at 17x; and 9-12% a year if the multiple never moves. This is step 6 of the argument.

Score: 82, set by the Rater. 20-35% gives B and +30% maps to about 85; placed down to 82 because two-thirds of the base return rests on a re-rating from 13.4x to 17x and the lower tail is fat (25% at (20)%), though earnings grow in every case and the three-year check is supportive.

#13 Summary conclusion

A quality compounder at a trough multiple with a mechanical EPS kicker the sell-side has not modelled; the risk is a structural, slow, hard-to-see cause for concern that may stop the re-rating short of the median.

Reply keeps the AI productivity gain that the rest of the sector is being forced to hand over. It is a 25-year compounder whose model (small fixed-price boutiques, onshore delivery, partners paid on margin) lets it retain that gain. Reply is spending the resulting cash on AI start-ups, a US foothold and a buyback of a tenth of its equity, at a multiple near its decade low.

The case's weakness is that the cause for concern, AI deflation, is structural, slow and unobservable from outside. The multiple may therefore stop reverting well short of its median, and the shares have already recovered 65% from the trough.

What to watch, in order.

  1. FY2026 results, 16 March 2027: H2 EBITDA margin at or above 18.3%, group organic growth at or above 7%, Germany at or above 4%, treasury shares above 5% of capital, and whether Region 3 EBIT is positive.
  2. Monthly buyback notices: at least €12m a month.
  3. Q1 2027 statement, mid-May 2027: organic growth, headcount growth at or above 5%, and the subcontractor ratio.
  4. H1 2027 results, late July 2027: Region 2 EBITDA margin toward 14%, Region 3 EBIT positive, average contract size, and the build-up of contract assets.
  5. Any US acquisition above €100m: its price, its margin and its effect on the buyback pace.
  6. Peers' disclosures on fixed-price share and deflation (Accenture has 65% fixed-price bookings; Capgemini; Sopra Steria), and Italian sovereign spreads.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 65, set by the Rater. Clearly positive inputs, a selective external tailwind (63) and a funded internal programme with a 10% buyback (70), reach profits only as about 12% EPS growth, barely above the Universe median, with margins flat near the past best and 3-4 points of it from the share count, so the net change is real but its profit step-up is moderate.

Foundations' Robustness: 74, set by the Rater. A 25-year compounder with a differentiated, capital-light model, ROIC near the top sixth, net cash and a long record of beating consensus makes the foundations robust, but a fragmented, hyperscaler-exposed industry facing an open AI-disruption question, entrenched governance and slow foreign turnarounds keep it just below the 75-80 band of the stable franchises.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 72, set by the Rater. The case fits 'CfC Clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a Q1 multiple' in substance (a clear cause for concern, a multiple at the bottom of its range, dated evidence of clearing), with a mechanical buyback upgrader element, but the cause for concern is structural and cannot be cleanly cleared by one print and current problems (Region 3 losses, German margin) blur it, so just below the 75 a clean trough-quality fit earns.

Case Riskiness: 62, set by the Rater. Fundamentally simple and low-risk (three trackable drivers, net cash, granular clients, a multiple low in its range), but the main risk of a large share-price fall is a slow, unobservable structural one (AI price deflation) amplified by sector sentiment swings and no guidance to anchor on, which is more than a paper cut, so it sits above the middle but well short of the 75-85 of boring, guided cases.

Default visuals are drawn from the Financial Analyst's model (update 1), FactSet and the Master Dashboard; history is FactSet's reported basis and forecasts are on the company/brokers' basis, so the step from the last actual year to the first forecast year can include a difference of basis. Charts in visuals/drawn take their figures from the memo. Consensus estimates are shown by named financial year.

Terms. "Cause for concern" (CfC) is the issue that has depressed the multiple. "Q1 multiple" means a multiple in the bottom quartile of the stock's own range. HQ and MQ mean high quality and medium quality. "Viewforth" denotes the Analyst's own forecasts in the charts.

Figures corrected

Every figure for Reply's past and reported results was checked against the Financial Analyst's model summary, using its bridge to the company's own reported figures (FY2025 revenue €2,483.6m, EBITDA €467.6m or 18.8%, EBIT €392.4m or 15.8%, net profit €250.9m, net cash €467.5m, H1 2026 margin 17.8%, H2 2025 margin 19.3%). The model's FY2023-25 columns are on a non-comparable FactSet basis and were not used to change any figure. Forecasts, scores and broker or FactSet consensus figures were left unchanged.
